hooks.text: Admiral Vernon minted medals celebrating a victory that never happened.
Why did London celebrate a victory while its fleet was being destroyed?
Admiral Vernon celebrated a triumph while his men were dying in disgrace.

title: Why Did the British Mint Medals for a Defeat? 🤯
description: In 1741, Admiral Vernon was so certain of victory at Cartagena that London minted medals for it, only to face a catastrophic disaster.

beats.text: Admiral Vernon minted medals celebrating a victory that never happened.
beats.visual: oil painting portrait of Admiral Edward Vernon, 1740
queries: Edward Vernon Royal Navy oil painting

beats.text: In 1741, London minted coins showing the Spanish commander kneeling in surrender.
beats.visual: 1741 bronze medal showing Blas de Lezo kneeling before Vernon
queries: The pride of Spain humiliated medal

beats.text: But the defender, Blas de Lezo, outmaneuvered the massive British fleet.
beats.visual: portrait painting of Admiral Blas de Lezo, 18th century

beats.text: Night assault failed when scaling ladders were ten feet too short.
beats.visual: engraving of the attack on Fort San Felipe de Barajas, 1741
queries: Castillo San Felipe de Barajas Cartagena

beats.text: Disease killed over 9,000 men during the sixty-seven-day siege.
beats.visual: engraving of 18th century British ships in a tropical harbor
queries: British ship of the line 18th century engraving

beats.text: The humiliation eventually collapsed the British government.
beats.visual: portrait of Prime Minister Robert Walpole, oil painting

beats.text: Those medals remained, celebrating a victory that never happened.
beats.visual: close up of the reverse of the 1741 Vernon medal

better_than_last: This script uses the myth_vs_fact structure to build tension before revealing the technical failure of the scaling ladders.
